sentences.text: Hylaeosaurus was about five meters long.
Gregory S. Paul estimated in 2010 that this animal weighed two tonnes.
The creature is described as having rows of armor plating on its back and tail, a long head, and a beak for cropping low vegetation.
Its head featured a triangular postorbital horn.
Maidment identified two unique traits: an unfused scapula and coracoid, along with three long shoulder spines.
The shoulder blade shows a sharp 120-degree angle between the acromion and the proximal plate.
The front shoulder spine is the longest, measuring 42.5 centimeters.
A fourth forward-pointing spine is located immediately behind the skull.
The skeleton was the most complete non-avian dinosaur known at the time of its discovery.
Hylaeosaurus was one of the first dinosaurs discovered, found in 1832 by Gideon Mantell.
Fossils were found in the Grinstead Clay.
On July 20, 1832, Mantell reported finding saurian bones in boulders freed by a gunpowder explosion at a quarry in Tilgate Forest.
In November 1832, Mantell decided to create the new generic name Hylaeosaurus.
On December 19, he chose the specific name armatus, meaning 'armed' or 'armoured', referring to the spikes and armor plates.
Gideon Mantell originally estimated that Hylaeosaurus was about 7.6 meters long.
Mantell originally modeled Hylaeosaurus after a modern lizard.
Only limited remains of Hylaeosaurus have been found, leaving much of its anatomy unknown.
Richard Owen based the classification of Dinosauria on Hylaeosaurus in 1842.
Coombs assigned Hylaeosaurus to the family Nodosauridae in 1978.
In the 1990s, some researchers mistakenly classified polacanthines like Hylaeosaurus as basal ankylosaurids due to a belief they had small tail clubs.
Hylaeosaurus armatus is currently the only valid species recognized in the genus.
Hylaeosaurus was the first ankylosaurian discovered, but its taxonomic affinities remained uncertain for a long time.
The parental group of Hylaeosaurus is the family Nodosauridae.
Hylaeosaurus lived from the Berriasian to the Albian, between 139.1 and 110.1 million years ago.
In 1840, Owen hypothesized that the asymmetrical spikes were not on the back but were incorrectly assumed to be gastralia or belly-ribs.
Mantell suggested that Hylaeosaurus either had a row of spines on its back forming a dermal fringe or possessed the same appendage on its tail.
It is debated whether Polacanthus is the same species as Hylaeosaurus armatus, despite differences in their osteology.
It is debated whether Hylaeosaurus was a basal nodosaurid or a basal ankylosaurian.
